articles.title: Neuroscientists uncover a universal mechanism for human decision making
articles.summary: When humans learn new rules, our brains use the exact same evidence-gathering process to make decisions as they do when processing basic physical sensations. A recent study shows that decision-making brain waves adapt to track arbitrary, newly learned categories.

articles.title: Genetic data indicates distinct metabolic pathways for different mental health disorders
articles.summary: People with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder often suffer from poor metabolic health. However, new research reveals their DNA actually aligns with favorable metabolic markers, pointing to medications and lifestyle as the true culprits.

articles.title: Distribird: Literature-Informed Prior Distribution Design for Bayesian Model Calibration
articles.summary: arXiv:2608.11210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian calibration of process-based models requires a prior distribution for each model parameter. We present \textbf{Distribird}, an agentic web application that automates this process. articles.title: The adult brain can repair itself better than scientists thought
articles.summary: The adult brain may be far better at repairing itself than scientists once believed. In mice, researchers discovered a special group of support cells called astrocytes that respond to damaged brain tissue by rebuilding lost cellular networks. Rather than simply moving into the injured area, these cells perform a remarkable maneuver: they create new nuclei and send them traveling through long cellular extensions to repopulate damaged regions.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden brain rhythm that could improve Parkinson’s treatment
articles.summary: Scientists have pinpointed a brain network—and its distinctive electrical rhythm—that appears to drive the benefits of deep brain stimulation for Parkinson’s disease. The discovery could lead to more precise, personalized stimulation settings and better results for patients.

articles.title: Breathing exercises blunt the body’s physical reaction to acute stress
articles.summary: Short breathing exercises can prevent sudden spikes in heart rate and anxiety. A new study reveals that just a few minutes of controlled breathing keeps physiological stress markers from rising when individuals face an intimidating social evaluation.

articles.title: LoKiFormer: Locality-aware Attention with Decoupled Knowledge Memory for Efficient Large Language Model Pretraining
articles.summary: arXiv:2608.12419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable breakthroughs across various applications. However, their architectures remain inefficient in pretraining due to two main limitations: (i) self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality, leading to redundant modeling of sequence-internal local information; (ii) mixture-of-experts (MoE) implicitly couples knowledge storage with computational pathways, hindering flexible access to sequence-external global knowledge. To overcome these limitations, we propose LoKiFormer, a novel LLM

articles.title: Which Site, and When: A Free-Satellite-Data Test of Himalayan Glacial Lake Bursts, Landslides, and Ice Floods
articles.summary: arXiv:2608.12422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two free satellite signals carry real information about glacial-lake outburst risk in the Nepal Himalaya: radar interferometry sees a moraine dam slowly sagging, and satellite weather marks the weeks when a primed lake is under stress. A companion feasibility study found that deformation indicates which lake is destabilizing and weather indicates when it is at risk, but proposed no predictive model. articles.title: Higher body fat in pregnancy may influence child ADHD risk through inflammation
articles.summary: A new study finds that higher maternal body fat during pregnancy increases systemic inflammation, which in turn predicts greater ADHD symptoms in toddlers. The findings highlight gestational inflammation as a potential pathway shaping early brain development.

articles.title: Trophic structure predicts seizure propagation in brain network models
articles.summary: arXiv:2608.12382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Epilepsy is widely regarded as a disorder driven by connectivity in the brain. We use a model of seizure dynamics on directed networks to investigate how structural properties affect seizure propensity. We find that properties such as trophic coherence, spectral radius, strong connectivity and non-normality are closely related to seizure propensity, and present a proof of a theoretical relationship between spectral radius and cycle structure. articles.title: A Bayes-Markov Neuromorphic Model of Cortical Orientation Selectivity: A Computational Re-implementation and Quantitative Simulation Study
articles.summary: arXiv:2608.12388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The emergence of orientation selectivity in the primary visual cortex (V1) remains a central question in computational neuroscience. Shirazi's Bayes-Markov model proposed a probabilistic explanation for how orientation-selective inhibition can arise from non-oriented lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) inputs through local inference. In that formulation, the activity pattern of striate cortical inhibitory (SCI) cells is estimated from the LGN activity pattern by a maximum a posteriori (MAP) criterion over a two-layer hierarchical Markov random field

articles.title: MIT neuroscientists discover the brain can reason without words
articles.summary: MIT neuroscientists have found striking evidence that language and logical reasoning are powered by separate systems in the brain. Even people with severe language impairments caused by stroke were able to solve challenging logic puzzles as well as people without those impairments, while brain scans showed that language-processing regions stayed largely quiet during reasoning tasks.
